traveler: Saint Mercurius of Caesarea (Philopator Mercurius, Abu Sayfayn, the Father of the Two Swords)
title: The Spear Taken Out of the Image: a Soldier of Cappadocia, His Two Dog-Headed Servants, and the Emperor He Killed a Hundred and Thirteen Years After His Own Death
years: c. 225-250, cult active to the present
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Hunt and the Dog-Headed Men

stops.name: Tomis, the Scythian house of the family
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source names a city for the family; Tomis stands here for the Scythian and Danubian frontier the texts evoke and nothing more. The Greek Passion (BHG 1274/1275) names the father Gordianos, primicerius of the Martenses; the Coptic and Arabic Acts name him Yares, baptized Noah. The contradiction between the two name traditions is recorded, not resolved. The year is a synthetic anchor one generation before the traditional birth of 225 and is not attested anywhere.
stops.campa: The house is Scythian, and it is military. Budge's summary of the Coptic martyrdom states it without ornament: the son of Gordianus, a native of Scythia. These men serve Rome along the cold northern edge of it, where the empire stops being a country and becomes a wall, and they serve it as pagans. The two traditions cannot agree what the father is called. The Greek Passion names him Gordianos and makes him primicerius of the regiment called the Martenses; the Coptic and Arabic Acts call him Yares. Neither tradition gives the family a city.
stops.quote: He was the son of Gordianus, a native of Scythia, and before he enlisted was known by the name of 'Philopator'.
stops.quote_source: E. A. Wallis Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts in the Dialect of Upper Egypt, vol. I (1915), Preface p. ix
suggested_refs: The Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275, pre-Metaphrastic, probably Cappadocian, 5th c. or later
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Preface p. ix
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774
R. Teja and S. Acerbi, 'Apuntes hagiograficos e iconograficos sobre San Mercurio'

stops.name: Cappadocia, the hunt and the two dog-headed men
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The episode survives only in the Coptic and Arabic Acts and the Synaxarium. Earlier working notes placed it in Egypt; Egypt is where the tradition was transmitted, not where it is set, and the narrative belongs to the Cappadocian family. No landmark is named in any version, so it is pinned at Caesarea, the nearest fixed point in the story. The year is a synthetic anchor.
stops.campa: Two men ride out after game, a father and a son, and the game is hunting them. Out of the scrub come two beings with the heads of dogs and the bodies of men. They take the elder man and eat him. They have the younger one down and are opening him when an angel stands in the field and draws a ring of fire around all three. Inside the ring the survivor promises what a man promises at that hour: belief, water, a son. He is baptized Noah. The dog-headed pair are still standing inside the fire when the story turns.
suggested_refs: R. Basset, Le Synaxaire arabe jacobite (1909)
A. Piankoff, 'Saint Mercure, Abou Seifein et les Cynocephales' (1942) and 'Deux Saints a la tete du chien' (1947)
sources: Coptic and Arabic Acts of Mercurius, summarized in Wikipedia, 'Ahrakas and Augani'
Teja and Acerbi, 'Apuntes hagiograficos e iconograficos sobre San Mercurio'

stops.name: Cappadocia, the two are named and kept
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The names Ahrakas and Augani (also Ahraqas and Oghani) are Coptic; they are not in the Greek Passion at all. The Coptic tradition is attested in the Synaxarium and in the surviving iconography, but the year here is a synthetic anchor, and no source dates the episode.
stops.campa: The two are not killed. They are broken, and then they are kept. The Synaxarium gives them names, Ahrakas and Augani, and puts them in the household as servants of the man whose father they ate. They are fed and lodged, and years later they go into battle behind his son's horse. Whether they are men from beyond the frontier or beasts that speak, no text reached here says. The Greek Passion does not have them at all; they exist only in the Coptic and Arabic Acts, and in the paint that follows those Acts.
suggested_refs: The eighteenth-century Coptic Museum icon attributed to Ibrahim al-Nasikh, the surviving image that names the pair
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ahrakas and Augani', citing Basset (1909), Piankoff (1942, 1947), Meinardus (1992)
Coptic Synaxarium tradition

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the promised son
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The birth year of 224 or 225 comes from later hagiographic compilation, not from any contemporary register; no third-century document about this man exists in any language. The birthplace Eskentos is named in the tradition and cannot be located on any reachable map, so the pin is the provincial seat.
stops.campa: The son promised inside the ring of fire is born at Eskentos in Cappadocia, to Noah and his wife Saphina, and they call him Philopator, lover of his father. The name pays a debt out loud. In the field the father bought his own life with a vow of a child not yet conceived, standing over what was left of his own father, and the child now carries the receipt for it. He is raised Christian in a province where that is a private matter and a legal risk. Eskentos is on no map anyone has reached. The house keeps two dog-headed servants.
suggested_refs: The Coptic and Arabic Acts of Mercurius, which alone supply the Eskentos birth and the mother's name
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Mercurius', summarizing the Greek Martyrdom and the Coptic and Arabic Acts
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the name given at enlistment
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and internally broken. The hagiography puts the enlistment at age seventeen and in the reign of Decius; Decius reigned only from September 249 to June 251, so a birth in 224 or 225 cannot yield a seventeen-year-old recruit under him. The year given here follows Decius rather than the age, which makes the recruit about twenty-five. A variant inside Budge's own volume has the name Mercurius given at baptism by a bishop rather than at the muster, so the naming scene itself is not stable.
stops.campa: He goes into the army as his father and his grandfather did, and at the muster the captain of his company writes down a new name for him. Philopator goes in; Mercurius comes out. The god the name belongs to is the guide of the dead and the patron of thieves and messengers, and it is now the legal name of a Christian soldier of Rome. He will carry both names for the rest of his life and long past the end of it. A variant inside Budge's own volume gives the name not at the muster but at baptism, from a bishop. Both readings are printed in the same book.
stops.quote: Gordianus called his son 'Philopator', but when the young man enlisted the captain of his company called him 'Mercurius'.
stops.quote_source: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Summaries p. cxv
suggested_refs: Budge's Coptic text of the Martyrdom, where a variant assigns the name at baptism rather than at enlistment
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Summaries p. cxv and Preface p. ix
Wikipedia, 'Decius'
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Satala, the regiment called the Martenses
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Passion names the unit, the province and the commander but no fort; Satala is a real, well attested Roman base in Late Roman Armenia Prima and stands here for the unnamed garrison. Armenia Prima as a province dates only from the Diocletianic reforms of about 293, decades after Decius, which is one of several signals that the text is not a court record. The month is arbitrary.
stops.campa: The unit is called the Martenses and it is posted in Armenia Prima, on the eastern frontier, under a commander named Satorninos. His father serves in the same regiment as primicerius. The war is against barbarians the Passion never names, in a campaign it never dates and on ground it never describes. What the text is precise about instead is the chain of command: unit, rank, commanding officer, promotion. Armenia Prima does not exist as a province until the reforms of about 293, forty years after Decius, and the Passion posts him there under Decius anyway.
suggested_refs: The Roman legionary fortress at Satala, Armenia Prima
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774
Wikipedia, 'Satala'
Wikipedia, 'Armenia Prima'

stops.name: Satala, the man in white with the sword
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The scene exists only inside the Greek Passion, which supplies no date and no place-name; the pin follows the garrison reconstruction above and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The night before the battle a man comes into the tent who is too large. He is dressed in white and he is carrying a sword, and he puts the sword into Mercurius's hands and tells him he will win with it, and then he gives him the condition: do not forget God. The soldier takes the weapon. Nothing in the Passion suggests he asks who the visitor is, and the Passion never says who it was. In the morning the army forms up, and the sword in his hand is not one that Rome issued him.
suggested_refs: The Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275, which alone preserves the swordbearer scene
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Satala, the barbarian king killed
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The Passion has the promotion conferred by Decius and Valerian jointly; Valerian did not rule with Decius, and this impossibility inside the source is the clearest internal evidence that the text is hagiography rather than a record of service. No battle answering this description is attested in any secular source. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: He finds the king of the barbarians in the field and kills him, and the war ends the way wars end in this kind of text: one man down, an army coming apart behind him. Decius promotes him to stratelates, general, over the heads of older officers. The Passion says the promotion came from Decius and Valerian together, as though the two men ruled at the same hour. No muster roll, no dispatch and no inscription survives that could correct it. He is a general, and by the reckoning of the tradition he is about twenty-five years old.
suggested_refs: The office of stratelates in the Late Roman command structure
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Satala, the second visit: the victory was the half of it
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Greek Passion only; undated in the source, pinned to the garrison and dated here to order the segment.
stops.campa: The visitor comes back to the same tent after the victory and takes the good news away again. Winning was half of it. The other half is that he is to be broken in public and killed for the name he has kept quiet at every muster since the day he enlisted. The Passion says that at this moment he remembers he is the son of Christians, which is a thing the text has him needing to be reminded of. It records no answer from him and no second question. The next scene is the sacrifice at the altar of Artemis, and he is late for it.
suggested_refs: The two-part vocation, victory then passion, as a structural device of the Greek military martyrdoms
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the cloak and the belt put off
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The Passion stages the confrontation before Decius in person and gives no date; Decius is not otherwise attested at Caesarea in Cappadocia. The date orders the segment. Caesarea is pinned at 38.7225, 35.4875, the canonical coordinates of Kayseri, and the same pin is used for every Caesarea stop in this file.
stops.campa: Ordered to sacrifice to Artemis, he takes off the general's cloak and unbuckles the military belt and puts them on the ground, which under Roman practice is not a gesture but a resignation, and he says he came into the world naked and can leave it the same way. Decius, whose court this is, is described in the text as furious and unable to stop looking at him: young, fair-haired, beautiful, brave. The emperor offers him the rank back. Everything that happens after this is done to a body with no rank on it.
suggested_refs: The cingulum militare, the Roman military belt, whose removal constituted formal discharge
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, four stakes and the fire under them
stops.date_confidence: legendary. First of the five tortures in the Greek Passion, all undated in the source; the sequence of dates in this segment records the order the text gives, not any calendar.
stops.campa: They stretch him between four stakes driven into the ground, and set a fire under him, and put swords into him while he hangs there. The blood comes out fast enough to put the fire out. It is the first of four tortures that will fail in the same manner, with the instrument working exactly as designed and the result coming out backwards. The Passion gives no date for it and no name for the man holding the swords. Nobody in the scene is converted yet. The executioners rake the coals back together and start again.
suggested_refs: The escalating-torture sequence as a formal feature of the Greek passiones
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the night the wounds close
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Greek Passion only, undated; the date orders the sequence.
stops.campa: He is carried into the prison more dead than alive and left there, which is the ordinary Roman method: no more men, no more fire, only time. In the night an angel comes and puts him back together. In the morning the guards bring out a man with no wounds on him. The Passion spends more words on Decius's astonishment than on the healing itself. It does not say what the guards said, or whether the men who opened the door in the morning were the men who had carried him in.
suggested_refs: Overnight angelic restoration as a recurring motif of the martyr passions
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the hot spears and the smell of the air
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Greek Passion only, undated; the date orders the sequence.
stops.campa: They heat spears in the fire and drive them through both his cheeks. What ought to happen next is the smell of burning meat in a closed room. What the text reports is a sweetness in the air, strong enough that the men doing the work notice it and say so aloud. The Passion has no interest in explaining this, and gives the scene a few lines before moving on to the next instrument. The same sweetness comes back in the room where they take his head off, and the Coptic text reports it there too.
suggested_refs: The odour of sanctity as an evidentiary sign in late antique martyr literature
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, hung head down under the stone
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Greek Passion only, undated; the date orders the sequence. The Passion places the court at Caesarea and then has him sent toward Cappadocia, which is where the court already is; the internal geography of the text does not close.
stops.campa: They hang him head downward with a stone tied on him and flog him until the floor under him is covered. The stone is the detail that puts the scene inside a real practice: it is there to stop the body swinging and to make the lungs work against the weight. He does not recant, and nothing he said under the stone is preserved. Decius, out of methods, orders him sent on to Cappadocia to be killed at home. The court is already sitting at Caesarea, in Cappadocia, and the text's own geography does not close.
suggested_refs: The internal geographic incoherence of the Greek Passion, noted by the Oxford Cult of Saints commentary
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Tyana, carried up the road on a pack animal
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The Passion says he was carried toward Caesarea on a pack animal and laid carefully at inns along the way, and names no inn and no town. Tyana is a real and well attested stage on the ancient road network of the region and stands here for those unnamed waystations. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He travels the last stretch of the road on a pack animal, laid down carefully at the inns along the way by the men escorting him, who have orders to deliver him alive to Caesarea and are handling a body that has been taken apart twice and put back together once. The road runs north through Tyana. It is a working imperial highway with milestones and stations, with grain and mail moving on it, and moving along it at the pace of a mule is the last month of his life. No text names the inns.
suggested_refs: The Roman road from the Cilician Gates through Tyana to Caesarea Mazaca
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, Christ comes in person
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The Greek Passion states that Christ appeared to Mercurius personally shortly before the execution and records nothing of what passed. Undated in the source; dated here immediately before the traditional martyrdom to order the segment.
stops.campa: At Caesarea, before the execution, Christ comes to him. Not an angel, and not the large man in white with the loaned sword: the Passion is specific that this last visit is made in person. What is said between them is not recorded. The soldier who was recruited by a stranger in a tent on the Armenian frontier is discharged by his actual commander in a cell in his own province. The Passion gives the fact of the visit, the place, and its nearness to the execution, and nothing else. It does not say whether he was alone in the cell.
suggested_refs: The Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275, on the personal appearance of Christ at Caesarea
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the beheading
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and the calendars disagree. The Coptic Orthodox calendar keeps the martyrdom on 25 Hathor, which falls on 4 December, and that is the date used here; the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox commemoration is 25 November, which is a feast and not a reported day of death. Earlier working notes fused the two into a single 25 November execution date, which no source supports. The year 250 is traditional and rests on no contemporary document.
stops.campa: They take his head off at Caesarea. The corpse turns white, the way the Coptic text keeps insisting, white as snow, and the sweetness that filled the room when they put the hot spears through his cheeks comes back and fills the whole place, and people who came out to watch an execution go home Christians. The tradition puts him at about twenty-five. The calendars will never afterward agree on which day this was: the Copts keep 25 Hathor, which falls on 4 December, and the Byzantines and the Latins keep 25 November.
suggested_refs: The Coptic Synaxarium under 25 Hathor; the Byzantine menologion under 25 November
sources: Greek Martyrdom of Merkourios, BHG 1274/1275
Wikipedia, 'Saint Mercurius', on the divergent feast and martyrdom dates
Coptic Orthodox liturgical calendar

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, buried in the gardens by the palace
stops.date_confidence: tradition. The burial in gardens near the royal palace comes from the hagiographic tradition as relayed in general reference accounts of the Passion; the ancient site is not independently verifiable and nothing above ground survives. The date follows the traditional martyrdom by one day and is an ordering device.
stops.campa: They put him in the ground in gardens near the royal palace at Caesarea, outside the walls of the city's official life and inside its most expensive district. Miracles start at the grave immediately, according to the tradition, which is the standard opening move of a martyr cult and is also, in this case, the only account there is of how the site came to be known at all. The gardens are not locatable now. Nothing above the ground survives that can be pointed at.
suggested_refs: The topography of late antique Caesarea Mazaca, modern Kayseri, where no shrine of Mercurius has been located archaeologically
sources: Hagiographic tradition summarized in general reference accounts of the Passion
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the poor man is told where the body lies
stops.date_confidence: legendary and undated. The vision-discovery of the body is pious legend layered onto an already legendary Passion; no source dates it and no contemporary account of any kind exists. The year is a synthetic anchor placed between the traditional martyrdom and the earliest textual stratum. Earlier working notes gave Caesarea as 38.7312, 35.4787; that value is dropped in favour of 38.7225, 35.4875 throughout.
stops.campa: A poor man in the city is visited and told where the body is. The visitor introduces himself by name and by title, Mercurius, the Martyr of the Lord, which is a form of words for an introduction and also, in a cult that will spend centuries insisting that this particular dead man does things, a statement of continuing employment. They dig where he says. The corpse is white as snow. It is taken into a church in the city first, and only later moved into a building of its own under his name.
suggested_refs: Vision-discovery of relics as a standard mechanism of late antique cult foundation
sources: Coptic and Byzantine hagiographic tradition, summarized at Wikipedia, 'Saint Mercurius'

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the bishop who does not mention him
stops.date_confidence: attested, and attested as an absence. Basil is bishop of Caesarea from 370 to 379 and is intensely engaged with the martyr shrines of his city in his homilies and letters; nowhere in his surviving corpus does he mention Mercurius. The Oxford Cult of Saints project records this silence directly. An attested silence is not proof that no cult existed in any form, and it is not treated here as one.
stops.campa: Basil is bishop here from 370 and he is the most articulate man in Cappadocia on the subject of martyrs. He preaches on their shrines and writes letters about their relics, and he organizes the veneration of the Forty of Sebaste in this very city. In everything of his that survives he never once mentions Mercurius. A century and a half after his death the legend will make this same Basil the eyewitness of the greatest story told about the saint. The Oxford Cult of Saints record notes the silence and stops there. A silence is not proof that no cult existed.
suggested_refs: Basil of Caesarea's homilies on the martyrs, and his cult of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste at Caesarea
sources: Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, commentary on record E02774
Oxford Reference, chronology of Basil of Caesarea, episcopate 370-379

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the pilgrim counts two names
stops.date_confidence: attested. Theodosius, De situ terrae sanctae, written shortly after 518, names Mercurius alongside Mamas as the great saints venerated at Caesarea in Cappadocia. This is the first solid external attestation of the cult. The year is the earliest possible date of composition; the text is not more precisely dated.
stops.campa: By the reign of Anastasius the shrine is on the itineraries. A pilgrim named Theodosius, setting down what a traveler to the Holy Land ought to see, lists what Caesarea in Cappadocia holds and gives it two names: Mamas, and Mercurius. That is the first solid sighting of the cult from outside its own literature. Between the beheading and that line lie two hundred and sixty-eight years in which nobody who was not writing hagiography mentions him at all.
suggested_refs: Theodosius, De situ terrae sanctae, early sixth-century pilgrim itinerary
The scholarly hypothesis deriving Merkourios from Kyrion of the Forty Martyrs of Sebaste by way of Mar Qurios, flagged by its own proposers as unproven
sources: Theodosius, De situ terrae sanctae, as discussed in Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E02774

segments.name: The Night of the Twenty-Sixth of June

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the spear taken out of the image
stops.date_confidence: legendary, on an attested date. The night is the attested night of Julian's death, 26 June 363. What happens at Caesarea on it is Coptic pseudo-Basilian legend, preserved in the Encomium (composition possibly sixth century, earliest dated manuscript Pierpont Morgan M.588, copied 842) and in Budge's translation. The quotation is verbatim from Budge, Preface p. x; earlier working notes cited p. xi in error.
stops.campa: On the night of the twenty-sixth of June the martyrium at Caesarea is quiet, and something happens inside it that the custodians only discover afterward. The saint comes out of his own shrine. Depending on the version, he steps out of the image on the wall, or off a painted tablet, or up out of the relics, and he takes the spear with him, because the spear is part of the picture and the picture is where he keeps it. What leaves the building is a Roman general in iron, a hundred and thirteen years dead.
stops.quote: Shall I permit this lawless man (i. e. Julian) to blaspheme the God of heaven in this manner?
stops.quote_source: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Preface p. x, reporting what Basil and his companions heard as Mercurius left the martyrium
suggested_refs: The Coptic pseudo-Basilian Encomium on Mercurius, Pierpont Morgan M.588, copied 842
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Preface p. x
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E01861
Teja and Acerbi, 'Apuntes hagiograficos e iconograficos sobre San Mercurio'

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, heaven opens over Basil's head
stops.date_confidence: legendary, and chronologically impossible as told. John Malalas, Chronographia, sixth century, is the earliest explicit version. The story requires Basil to be bishop of Caesarea on the night of 26 June 363; Basil was not consecrated until 370. The seven-year gap is recorded here as a property of the legend, not adjudicated, and not smoothed over: the myth needs the two great Cappadocians, apostate emperor and Christian bishop, already in their finished roles.
stops.campa: In Malalas's version Basil is at prayer when the sky comes apart over Caesarea, and he sees Christ enthroned, and hears the order given aloud and by name to a soldier standing in the court: go and kill Julian, who blasphemes me. Mercurius is wearing polished iron. He goes out, and he comes back, and he reports the way a junior officer reports, that the emperor has been struck down as commanded. Basil is not alone in the room. The text puts companions there with him, and they hear it too.
suggested_refs: John Malalas, Chronographia, on the reign and death of Julian
Simon Binon, Essai sur le cycle de Saint Mercure, martyr de Dece et meurtrier de l'empereur Julien (1937)
sources: John Malalas, Chronographia, sixth century
Teja and Acerbi, 'Apuntes hagiograficos e iconograficos sobre San Mercurio'
Oxford Reference, chronology of Basil of Caesarea

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the figure leaves the painted tablet
stops.date_confidence: legendary, and a separate transmission. The Arabic chronicler Eutychius, Sa'id ibn Batrik, tenth century, gives an independent variant of the icon motif in which the spear returns with blood on the tip. Budge quotes it at Preface p. xi and cites Pococke's Contextio Gemmarum, sive Eutychii Annales (Oxford, 1656), i, 484-7. Same night as the Malalas vision; a different account of the same claim.
stops.campa: The Arabic chronicler Sa'id ibn Batrik tells it with the furniture rearranged. Basil is sitting in his chair with a painted tablet propped in front of him and the figure of Mercurius on it, and he is looking straight at it when the figure goes out of the picture. The panel stays blank for an hour. When the figure comes back there is blood on the point of the spear it holds, and Basil sits there unable to speak until the news arrives and gives him the hour. The Ethiopic version says only that the spear was full of blood.
stops.quote: In the Annals of Sa'id ibn Batrik, or Eutychius, it is said that Basil was sitting on his chair, with a tablet in front of him on which a figure of Mercurius was painted. Whilst he was looking the figure of Mercurius disappeared from the tablet... When it returned Basil saw that on the tip of the spear... there was blood, and Basil remained stupefied with astonishment until he heard later that Julian had been slain at that hour.
stops.quote_source: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Preface p. xi, reporting Eutychius
suggested_refs: Pococke, Contextio Gemmarum, sive Eutychii Annales (Oxford, 1656), i, 484-7
Abu Salih, ed. Evetts, p. 161; Butler, Coptic Churches, ii, p. 359
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Preface p. xi
Eutychius (Sa'id ibn Batrik), Annals, tenth century

stops.name: Maranga on the Tigris, the spear in the emperor's side
stops.date_confidence: attested. Ammianus Marcellinus, a serving officer on the campaign, describes the wounding in Res Gestae XXV.iii. The exact site is disputed and unlocated; the coordinates are those of Samarra and approximate the region of the retreat near Maranga. Ammianus names no attacker at all, and does not mention Mercurius.
stops.campa: The emperor is on the retreat up the Tigris, harried the whole way, and word comes that the rear of the column is under attack. He goes out to it without stopping for his cuirass. A cavalry spear takes him in the side, through the ribs and into the liver. He grabs the shaft with his right hand and cuts his own fingers open on the blade, and falls off the horse, and is carried to his tent. The man who wrote this down was on the march with him and does not say who threw the spear.
stops.quote: a cavalry spear, grazing the skin of his arm, pierced his side, and fixed itself in the bottom of his liver. He tried to pull it out with his right hand, and cut the sinews of his fingers with the double-edged point of the weapon; and, falling from his horse, he was borne with speed by the men around him to his tent
stops.quote_source: Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae XXV.iii, translated at tertullian.org/fathers/ammianus_25_book25.htm
suggested_refs: Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae, Books XXIII-XXV, the Persian campaign of 363
sources: Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae XXV.iii
Wikipedia, 'Julian (emperor)'
Wikipedia, 'Battle of Samarra'

stops.name: The camp on the Tigris, blood thrown at the sky
stops.date_confidence: legendary against attested. The dying words are the Coptic addendum to the Martyrdom, translated in Budge, Preface p. x. Ammianus, present in the camp, has Julian discussing the nobility of the soul with two philosophers and expiring quietly about midnight of the same night he was struck; earlier working notes said he died days later, which Ammianus contradicts. The date here is the small hours after the wounding.
stops.campa: In the Coptic telling there is no doubt at all about who threw it. The spear goes through the loins, and the emperor, lying in the tent with his hands full of his own blood, throws a handful of it up into the air and says what he says, and dies. Ammianus, who was in the camp that night, has him spend his last hours discussing the nobility of the soul with two philosophers and going quiet about midnight. Ammianus records no shout and no blood thrown in the air, and the Coptic text records no philosophers.
stops.quote: Take this, O Christ, for Thou hast taken the whole world.
stops.quote_source: Coptic addendum on Julian's death appended to the Martyrdom of Mercurius, translated in Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Preface p. x
suggested_refs: The Coptic addendum on the death of Julian appended to the Martyrdom of Mercurius
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Preface p. x
Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae XXV.iii.23

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the weapon is missing from the shrine
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Budge's Coptic version says the messenger sent to the martyrium found the spear missing, and adds explicitly that three days later the news of Julian's death arrived and that nothing is said about the spear coming back. The bloodied-spear-returned motif belongs to the Arabic Eutychius variant and to the Ethiopic version, not to this one. The date is three days after the death, per Budge.
stops.campa: In the morning they send someone to the martyrium to look at the image, and the spear is not in it. Budge's summary is careful about what happens next and about what does not: three days later the news of Julian's death reaches Caesarea, and about the spear, nothing further is said. It does not come back in this version. The custodian is left standing in front of a painted figure with an empty hand, three days before anyone in Caesarea knows what happened on the Tigris.
suggested_refs: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Preface pp. x-xi, on what the Coptic version does and does not say about the spear
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Preface pp. x-xi
Coptic pseudo-Basilian tradition, Oxford Cult of Saints record E01861

stops.name: Caesarea in Cappadocia, the vow of Agathonicus
stops.date_confidence: legendary. The Coptic pseudo-Basilian Encomium retrojects the shrine enlargement into the reign of Jovian, immediately after Julian's death, which fixes the narrative year at 363-364; the episode has no independent attestation. The whole miracle cycle in this segment is set at a shrine the Coptic text places at Caesarea and the manuscript tradition also associates with Egyptian foundations, and that ambiguity is not resolved here.
stops.campa: A man named Agathonicus promises to make the shrine bigger. Then he does what men do with promises made in gratitude, which is nothing, for long enough that the promise becomes a memory. Mercurius comes to him in his sleep and puts the matter to him as one officer to another: an unfulfilled vow is a debt owed to a party who is present. Building starts the next day. The Coptic text sets this in the reign of Jovian, directly after Julian's death, with the emperor dealt with and the general back on his own site. Nothing outside the Encomium attests any of it.
suggested_refs: The overcrowded three-day shrine festival of the same cycle, at which the preacher had to break off his sermon and Mercurius disciplined, threatened, healed and enforced promises in person
sources: Coptic pseudo-Basilian Encomium on Mercurius, Pierpont Morgan M.588
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E01861
Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I

stops.name: The shrine under construction, the ox that gored its fellow
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Fourth Miracle of the Coptic Encomium, undated in the source; the quotation is verbatim from Budge, Summaries p. cxx, where the companion healing appears on the same page. Earlier working notes cited p. cxxi in error. The date orders the cycle.
stops.campa: There are oxen on the site hauling stone, and one of them puts a horn into the flank of the one working beside it. The saint arrives, in person, and touches the wounded animal with his foot, and the wound is not there any more. Then he turns to the other one. The sentence he hands down is not death; it is confiscation of the instrument. The horns start to rot on the animal's head and come off it, and after that the beast is quiet and works well and gives nobody any trouble on the site.
stops.quote: The saint then went and rebuked the ox which had gored its fellow, and told it that its horns should fall out; and straightway the horns began to decay, and they fell off its head, and the animal became quiet and docile.
stops.quote_source: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Summaries p. cxx, Fourth Miracle
suggested_refs: The Coptic Encomium's miracle cycle as a record of shrine construction practice
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Summaries p. cxx
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E01861

stops.name: The shrine under construction, the stolen plank
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Sixth Miracle of the Coptic Encomium, undated in the source; the quotation runs from the foot of Budge, Summaries p. cxxi onto p. cxxii. Earlier working notes cited pp. cxxii-cxxiii in error. The date orders the cycle.
stops.campa: A man walks off the site with a plank of construction timber on his shoulder, headed home. The saint takes his mind away from him, gently, the way you turn a horse. The thief walks to the house of the custodian of the shrine instead, and stands outside it under the weight of the beam, staggering about with not the least idea where he is. When it comes back to him he confesses in front of everybody. He spends the rest of the build mixing mud and making bricks, unpaid.
stops.quote: A certain man stole a plank of wood from the timber which was being used in the construction of the shrine of Mercurius, and whilst he was carrying it to his house the saint made his mind to wander, and made him to go to the house of the custodian of the shrine
stops.quote_source: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Summaries pp. cxxi-cxxii, Sixth Miracle
suggested_refs: The Coptic Encomium's treatment of theft, vows and restitution at the shrine
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Summaries pp. cxxi-cxxii
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E01861

stops.name: The shrine under construction, the beam that fruits
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Coptic Encomium, undated in the source; quotation verbatim from Budge, Summaries p. cxxiii. The date orders the cycle.
stops.campa: A workman, tired, makes a joke out loud about the timber going up in the apse: let it put out branches, let it fruit, let it feed the men lifting it. The joke is taken seriously by the party it was addressed to. Branches come out of the seasoned wood, and fruit comes with the branches, and the workmen see that the boughs are loaded. They eat on the site. People carry pieces of the fruit home afterward and keep them as phylakteria, and Budge's summary says that many cures were effected by it.
stops.quote: were the words spoken when branches began to grow out of the wood, and the workmen saw that they were laden with fruit... many people brought away some of the fruit and kept it as phylacteries, and many cures were effected by it.
stops.quote_source: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Summaries p. cxxiii
suggested_refs: Phylakteria, amulets made from shrine material, in the Coptic healing economy
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Summaries p. cxxiii
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E01861

stops.name: The shrine, Gaipios on his mule
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Seventh and Eighth Miracles of the Coptic Encomium, undated in the source; quotation from Budge, Summaries pp. cxxiii-cxxiv. The episode is anti-Jewish polemic of a kind standard in the genre, and it is reported here as the text has it, not endorsed. The date orders the cycle.
stops.campa: Gaipios rides his mule into the martyrium to see the miracles for himself and to say what he thinks of them, which he does, in the middle of the workmen. The saint comes out and runs him through with the spear. What follows is not a death; it is a negotiation. Gaipios, on the floor, offers to pay for an image. He is healed and baptized Zacharias, his wife becomes Elisabeth, the twin sons are named Mercurius and John, and the stele he commissions is gold, inlaid with stones, and shows the saint spearing him.
stops.quote: St. Mercurius came and drove the spear which he had in his hand into the body of Gaipios, and rebuked him for bringing the mule into the church, and for obstructing the workers in his shrine.
stops.quote_source: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Summaries pp. cxxiii-cxxiv
suggested_refs: The miracle that commissions its own cult image: the Gaipios stele
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Summaries pp. cxxiii-cxxiv
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E01861

stops.name: The shrine, the daughter of Hermapollo
stops.date_confidence: legendary. Coptic Encomium, undated in the source; summarized in Budge and in the Oxford Cult of Saints record E01861. The date orders the cycle.
stops.campa: A young man is refused and hires a magician, and the daughter of Hermapollo falls ill in the way girls fall ill in these texts, which is to say deliberately and from a distance. Mercurius comes at night in the character the Copts always give him, a general in a rage with the sword already out, and hits the young man three times with the flat of it, and makes him undo what he paid for. Then he arranges the marriage. The father sends a ceremonial bier to the shrine: ivory, precious stones, crosses of gold and silver.
suggested_refs: Donation of liturgical furniture as the standard settlement of a miracle debt in the Coptic cycle
sources: Coptic pseudo-Basilian Encomium on Mercurius
Oxford Cult of Saints in Late Antiquity, record E01861
Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I

stops.name: Edfu, the body that walks and the mule that speaks
stops.date_confidence: legendary, and the place is contested inside the tradition itself. Budge's Edfu manuscript (British Library Oriental MS 6802, judged by its editor probably eleventh century) sets the walking corpse at Edfu in Upper Egypt; the earlier cycle sets it narratively at Caesarea. The pin follows Caesarea, with the Edfu attribution recorded here rather than invented as a coordinate. The quotation is verbatim from Budge, Preface p. ix, and appears again in the Summaries at p. cxix; earlier working notes cited p. x, which is wrong.
stops.campa: The corpse gets up and walks into the city on its own feet, with the crowd singing on both sides of the road, and there is a mule in the procession that has the gift of human speech and uses it. A man tries to turn the procession into his own house, to have the body under his roof and the cures that come with it. The body becomes too heavy to move. The bearers stand in the road under it until he gives the idea up, and then it goes on as before. Budge's Edfu manuscript puts the walk in Upper Egypt; the earlier cycle puts it at Caesarea.
stops.quote_source: The talking mule, in Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I (1915), Preface p. ix; repeated in the Summaries at p. cxix, Third Miracle
suggested_refs: British Library Oriental MS 6802, the Edfu manuscript of the Martyrdom and Miracles of Mercurius the General
British Library Oriental MS 6801, whose colophon is too mutilated for its date to be recovered
sources: Budge, Miscellaneous Coptic Texts, vol. I, Preface p. ix and Summaries p. cxix
Budge, preface description of Oriental MSS 6801-6802

stops.name: Alexandria, the relics come down into Egypt
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and undated. The Coptic Synaxarium commemorates a translation of part of the relics on 9 Paoni, 16 June, following contact between an Armenian Catholicos and the Patriarch of Alexandria. No year, no route and no named agent survives; the year 700 here is a synthetic anchor that orders the segment and is asserted by nobody. Relic-translation narratives of this shape are devotional tradition and are not treated as documented events.
stops.campa: Part of him is carried down into Egypt. The tradition says the transfer was arranged between the Catholicos of Armenia and the Patriarch of Alexandria, and it gives the day, 9 Paoni, the sixteenth of June, and no year, no route and no name for the man who carried the box. Egypt receives a Cappadocian general in the reign of nobody in particular and keeps the anniversary in the calendar from then on. What arrives is not the whole body. The Coptic sources are careful to say part.
suggested_refs: The Coptic Synaxarium under 9 Paoni
sources: Coptic Synaxarium tradition, summarized at Wikipedia, 'Saint Mercurius'
Coptic Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Dayr Abu Sayfayn'

stops.name: Old Cairo, the enclosure north of the fortress
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the complex, reconstruction as to the year. The Saint Mercurius church and the Dayr Abu Sayfayn enclosure stand just north of the Babylon fortress in Old Cairo at 30.012444, 31.230806; earlier working notes gave 30.0043, 31.2308 and 30.0059, 31.2302, both of which fall inside Qasr al-Sham and contradict the Coptic Encyclopedia's own 'north of Qasr al-Sham'. The enclosure wall is attributed to a twelfth century patron whose name appears as Ibn Abu al-Fada'il ibn Faruj and also as ibn Faruq; the spelling is not settled and 1150 is a midpoint standing for 'in the course of the twelfth century', not a documented year. The Coptic Encyclopedia entry could not be re-verified directly in this pass.
stops.campa: North of the fortress at Babylon, in the town the Arabs built at Fustat, there is a walled enclosure with three churches and a convent of nuns inside it, and the whole precinct is called after him: Dayr Abu Sayfayn, the house of the Father of the Two Swords. His church is the largest building in the district of ancient Babylon. The enclosure wall goes up in the twelfth century at the expense of a man the Coptic Encyclopedia names Ibn Abu al-Fada'il ibn Faruj. Teja and Acerbi count more than twenty-five churches to him across Egypt.
suggested_refs: A. J. Butler, The Ancient Coptic Churches of Egypt, vol. 1 (Oxford, 1884), pp. 75-76, describing the enclosure and the churches of Saint Shenute and the Virgin within it
J. Vansleb, Nouvelle Relation en forme de journal d'un voyage fait en Egypt en 1672 et 1673 (Paris, 1677), on the patriarchal precinct near Qasr al-Sham
The old sycamore-wood enclosure door, iron-banded, now Coptic Museum inventory 688
sources: Coptic Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Dayr Abu Sayfayn' (Charalambia Coquin)
Wikipedia, 'Saint Mercurius Church in Coptic Cairo'
Wikipedia, 'Coptic Cairo'
Teja and Acerbi, 'Apuntes hagiograficos e iconograficos sobre San Mercurio'

stops.name: Old Cairo, the patriarch writes out the whole name
stops.date_confidence: attested. The History of the Patriarchs, treating the tenure of Mark VII (30 May 1745 to 18 May 1769), names 'the monastery of the great martyr Philopator Mercurius, Father of the Two Swords'. The date given here is the start of that patriarchate; the History itself is a compiled chronicle, medieval to early modern.
stops.campa: The History of the Patriarchs, keeping its account of the tenure of Mark VII, has occasion to name the place, and writes it out in full: the monastery of the great martyr Philopator Mercurius, Father of the Two Swords. Both names are still on him fifteen centuries after the captain of a Roman company crossed one out and wrote the other in, and the epithet is a third name, earned after death, for a weapon he was handed twice. Mark VII is patriarch from 1745 to 1769.
suggested_refs: The History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria, on Patriarch Mark VII
sources: Coptic Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Dayr Abu Sayfayn', citing the History of the Patriarchs

stops.name: Old Cairo, the convent and the confiscation order
stops.date_confidence: reported, contemporary, and undated in the source. Wikipedia's article on Saint Mercurius reports the abbess as Tenmav Irini, the confiscation as being for the Ministry of Defence, and the reversal as attributed to President Hosni Mubarak, whose presidency ran 1981 to 2011; the year 1990 is a placeholder inside that span and is asserted by nobody. This is a present-day devotional claim, not a verified event.
stops.campa: The Ministry of Defence moves to take land belonging to the convent inside the enclosure. The nuns and their abbess, Tenmav Irini, do what the Coptic sources have described people doing at this address for a thousand years, which is to take the matter to him directly. The order is reversed. The reversal is announced in the president's name and credited inside the convent to the saint, which is the same personality the miracle cycle records handling the same category of problem. No year appears in the source, and no document of the confiscation was reached here.
suggested_refs: The Abu Sefein convent at Dayr Abu Sayfayn, Old Cairo, still in occupation
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Mercurius', reporting modern devotional accounts from the Abu Sefein convent

stops.name: Benevento, the relics that are not his
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date, attested as to the confusion. Hippolyte Delehaye identified the Benevento relics as those of Mercurius of Aeclanum, a distinct saint, and Christopher Walter followed him; Walter's text was not reachable in this pass (403 on the available copy) and the identification is reproduced from the operator's brief citing him. No source reached here dates the arrival of the relics at Benevento, and the year given is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: There are relics under an altar at Benevento labelled with his name, and they are not his. Delehaye separated them and Christopher Walter followed him: the bones belong to Mercurius of Aeclanum, a different saint out of a different town, absorbed into the Cappadocian soldier's file by the same ordinary process that gave the Cappadocian soldier a Scythian grandfather and two dog-headed servants. Nobody at Benevento was deceived by anyone. Nothing in the reachable record says when the confusion started.
suggested_refs: Hippolyte Delehaye on the doublets of the military martyrs
Christopher Walter, The Warrior Saints in Byzantine Art and Tradition
sources: Christopher Walter, The Warrior Saints in Byzantine Art and Tradition, following Delehaye, as cited in the operator's brief

stops.name: Faras, the emperor under the hooves
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the painting, approximate as to the year. The Faras cathedral mural showing Mercurius mounted and spearing Julian is dated to the ninth century in the iconographic literature; no closer date is offered by the sources reached. The site is now under Lake Nasser and the plaster is in museum collections in Khartoum and Warsaw.
stops.campa: On a wall of the cathedral at Faras, in Nubia, somebody paints him the way the south will paint him from now on: up on the horse, spear down, and the emperor of Rome under the hooves. This is the ninth century. The composition is the one the Greeks use for George and the dragon, with the dragon taken out and Julian put in its place. The cathedral is under Lake Nasser now. The plaster was cut off the walls before the water came up and is in museums at Khartoum and Warsaw.
suggested_refs: Christopher Walter, The Warrior Saints in Byzantine Art and Tradition
The Faras Gallery, National Museum in Warsaw
sources: Teja and Acerbi, 'Apuntes hagiograficos e iconograficos sobre San Mercurio'
Standard iconographic scholarship on the Faras cathedral murals

stops.name: Hosios Loukas, standing in a row with the other soldiers
stops.date_confidence: attested. The katholikon at Hosios Loukas is tentatively dated 1011-1012 and holds the best preserved mosaic complex of the Macedonian renaissance; Mercurius appears there among the military saints. Earlier working notes gave the coordinates as 38.4166, 22.9351, which lie about eighteen kilometres east, out toward Livadeia, and are corrected here. A fresco of 1295 at Ohrid is reported in the same connection and is left in the references rather than given a coordinate of its own.
stops.campa: In the Greek world he is not on a horse. In the katholikon at Hosios Loukas, built in the first years of the eleventh century, he stands in the mosaic among the other military saints, upright, armed, decorative, an ornament of the imperial order rather than an instrument used against an emperor. The Byzantines who kept his feast on the twenty-fifth of November had the Julian story in their own chronicles and did not put it on their walls. Egypt painted him riding; Greece stood him up in a row.
suggested_refs: The reported fresco of 1295 in a church at Ohrid, North Macedonia
Christopher Walter, The Warrior Saints in Byzantine Art and Tradition, on the standing military saint type
sources: Wikipedia, 'Saint Mercurius'
Wikipedia, 'Hosios Loukas'

stops.name: Monastery of Saint Anthony, the whole story in one field of paint
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the fresco, loose as to the year. The fresco at the Monastery of Saint Anthony on the Red Sea is dated in the literature only to a range of roughly the tenth to thirteenth centuries; 1100 is a midpoint standing for that range. Meinardus (1992) proposed an Armenian origin for the cynocephali icon type.
stops.campa: At the monastery on the Red Sea the scene is assembled complete. Mercurius is mounted; Julian is on the ground under the horse; an angel is coming in from the side with a second sword, which is where the epithet comes from; and behind the horse, doing their own work on a human figure, are the two dog-headed men out of the hunt his father survived. Four centuries of story stand in one field of paint, in the order the Synaxarium tells them. Nothing in the picture explains itself to anyone who has not heard it. The fresco is dated in the literature only to somewhere between the tenth century and the thirteenth.
suggested_refs: O. F. A. Meinardus (1992) on the Cynocephali icon and its proposed Armenian origin
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ahrakas and Augani', citing Meinardus (1992)
Teja and Acerbi, 'Apuntes hagiograficos e iconograficos sobre San Mercurio'

stops.name: Lalibela, the church cut out of the rock in his name
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the church, reported only as to the iconography. Biete Qeddus Mercoreus is confirmed as one of the eleven rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, and King Lalibela reigned about 1181 to 1221, so the date holds. The name Oleonus as the Ethiopian form of Julian, the black horse and the cynocephalic attendants in the Ethiopian program could not be confirmed in any accessible source and are given here as reported tradition, following Teja and Acerbi, whose page reference was not obtainable.
stops.campa: In the rock at Lalibela one of the eleven churches is cut out and given his name, Biete Qeddus Mercoreus, and in the Ethiopian telling he rides a black horse. The figure under the spear is called Oleonus in that tradition, and the tradition says Oleonus is Julian. King Lalibela reigns from about 1181 to 1221 and the churches belong to his reign. The stone is a single piece. The church was made by taking away everything that was not the church, and pilgrims still come down the trench to the door.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela', on Biete Qeddus Mercoreus
sources: Teja and Acerbi, 'Apuntes hagiograficos e iconograficos sobre San Mercurio'
Wikipedia, 'Rock-Hewn Churches, Lalibela'

stops.name: Coptic Museum, Old Cairo, the panel that names the dog-headed pair
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the icon, approximate as to the year. The eighteenth-century icon in the Coptic Museum is attributed to Ibrahim al-Nasikh, whose documented workshop partner Yuhanna al-Armani lived 1726 to 1786; earlier working notes called al-Armani a seventeenth-century painter, which is wrong. The year 1750 stands for the middle of their working lives and is not a documented date of production.
stops.campa: An icon painted in Cairo in the eighteenth century, attributed to Ibrahim al-Nasikh, fixes the Coptic formula in the shape it will keep: the young general on a dark horse, two crossed swords, the spear, Julian on the ground, and Basil at the side of the picture watching the vision he is having. It is also the surviving image that puts the names Ahrakas and Augani on the dog-headed pair. Al-Nasikh's workshop partner Yuhanna al-Armani lived from 1726 to 1786, and the panel is placed by that association rather than by any date on it.
suggested_refs: Yuhanna al-Armani's depiction of Mercurius associated with the Hanging Church, al-Muallaqa, Old Cairo
Danijela Stefanovic and A. Piankoff on the cynocephali in Coptic art
sources: Wikipedia, 'Ahrakas and Augani', citing the Coptic Museum attribution to Ibrahim al-Nassikh
